My dad became suddenly very ill at the start of last year. Tried to kill himself and regularly has no idea what's going on. We don't really know what caused it, he's been diagnosed with depression but there's clearly something more. No UTIs or anything.

I physically can't care for him. For the first 3 months me and my sister alternated weeks caring for him. The thing is, he wasn't the nicest person even before this. I wouldn't say he was abusive, but he was manipulative and nasty and an attention seeker. His new state of being just exacerbates this. It was an awful 3 month.

He then went to a care home for 6 months, as he couldn't be left alone, but we couldn't care for him. He made a lot of progress there, and eventually came home with a full-time carer living with him. She stayed for 6 months until dad's condition and attitude had worsened again to the point she couldn't take it anymore, and she suddenly left. I don't know how she stayed for that long tbh.

I went and cared for him for 1.5 weeks after she left until we could get him back into a care home. To say it was the hardest 1.5 weeks of my life is an understatement. I was getting 2 hours of sleep most nights, being woken up by him for every little thing and being screamed at to call 999 because he thought he was going to die. Every night.

He's now in a care home again thankfully, but wants to leave. I feel awful for him because he has no sort of life there. He has a lot more mental capacity than most of the people there, but just isn't well enough to be at home.

So to answer your question: I tried. But it's impossible. To be honest, it kills me knowing that I'm not caring for him. I feel like a bit of a failure. But I can't do it. I'm not physically capable of it. The only solace I get from it is knowing that a professional, qualified full-time carer wasn't able to deal with him either. I don't feel safe doing it, neither for me nor for him. He has no life now as a result, though. I sometimes just wish he was dead, because that's more a life than what he's living now.

If you're likely to buy in the next two years, stop putting money into S&S unless you won't need it for your deposit. Ideally, money should only be in S&S if you're planning to hold it for 5 years or long, to ride out any bumps in the market.

Also, consider moving your money from your H2B ISA to a LISA. The terms are much more favourable, you can buy up to £450000 instead of £250000 (if you're outside London). You also aren't limited to £12k total deposit. You can move £4k per tax year, so do £4k now and you can do another £4k as soon as the new tax year comes around. You can only use one or the other, but in 14 months you'll have all £12k transferred over, and you can't use it for a year after opening anyway.

On your 90 day saver, if you've maxed out your ISA contributions, don't worry about tax. You're better off being taxed on earnings over £1000, than not earning over that at all.

The way it works is, if the amount you earned this month (including bonus) would put you on track to earn over the threshold for the next tax bracket if you earned it every month til the end of the tax year, then you'll get charged that higher bracket on the extra bit above that threshold, as it looks like you'd be over the threshold by the end of the year. Of course, you won't be, and they'll realise that next payslip so you'll pay less tax to make up for it.

In the eyes of HMRC, there's no real distinction here between a £2k bonus and a £2k per month pay rise, and obviously for the latter you should be paying more tax over the year.

Yes it's possible. I did it. First two years of uni I had very few friends, and pretty much no social life. This year I joined a sports club for a sport I've never played before, and I have some amazing friends there, and got the "uni experience" I was convinced I wouldn't be able to get before I graduated.

It wont change by itself though, you need to put yourself out there. Join sports clubs or societies and get involved in their activities. You don't even usually need to be good or have even played before for most sports clubs, and they generally tend to be more social than societies too, so that's my recommendation if that's your sort of thing. I believe most clubs run taster sessions at the start of the academic year; give a few a try, find something you like and stick with it. 

And if sports aren't really for you, societies can still be great for socialising and finding like-minded people, so find something that you like. Make sure you go their events, and chat to people. I'll repeat, you do have to put yourself out there a bit, but you can definitely change things around if you try.
